# FTAI Aviation Ltd. (FTAI) — Forensic Dossier
**Interrogator pass · 2026-07-16 · five consecutive quarterly calls (Q1 2025 → Q1 2026)**
**Price used: $199.93 (NASDAQ, USD, live quote 2026-07-16) · market value ~$20.5B · ~103M shares**

---

## 1. NARRATIVE ARC

FTAI rebuilds used jet engines. Its core idea is genuinely clever: instead of an airline sending a worn CFM56 engine (the workhorse on older Boeing 737s) into a traditional repair shop for a months-long, multi-million-dollar overhaul, FTAI hands them a rebuilt engine off the shelf and takes the tired one back. Management calls this "maintain, repair and exchange." Airlines save time and money; FTAI earns a spread on the swap.

Across the five calls the story did not merely evolve — it kept acquiring new legs, and each new leg arrived before the previous one had been proven in cash.

**Q1 2025 — one business, one goal.** The pitch was tight and testable: aerospace products earning $131 million in quarterly adjusted earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortization (EBITDA — a rough proxy for operating profit) at a 36% margin, market share going "beyond the current 5% to 25%," and a new outside fund, the Strategic Capital Initiative, that would buy the aircraft so FTAI would not have to. The company committed to "$650 million in adjusted free cash flow for all of 2025."

**Q2 2025 — the ambitions inflate.** Share doubled to 9%. The cash-flow target was raised from $650 million to $750 million. Two acquisitions were announced. And the promise that anchors everything since: "we continue to expect Aerospace Products margins to expand to the 40% plus range in 2026."

**Q3 2025 — the fund becomes the story.** The Strategic Capital Initiative doubled from $3 billion to $6 billion. Mr. Adams reframed the company entirely: "we have 2 businesses. 1 is a factory that makes engines and the other is an asset manager." An asset manager is valued very differently from an engine shop — this was a deliberate multiple-expansion argument, not just a description.

**Q4 2025 — a third leg appears.** FTAI Power: converting retired jet engine cores into gas turbines for data centres. No customer named, no order book, no revenue. Asked directly whether an order book exists, management said only that they are "talking to hyperscalers" and "it's not the right time from a commercial standpoint" to say more.

**Q1 2026 — the pivot in plain sight.** Revenue in aerospace products grew 104% year over year. Margin fell to 30%. The 40%-plus promise was not withdrawn, defended, or even mentioned. It was replaced, in the same breath, with its opposite: 30% margins are "indicative of an increased mix of deals with large airline customers and a larger mix of full performance restoration shop visits. **We expect this to be the trend line going forward.**"

That sentence is the most important in five calls, and I return to it in section 4.

---

## 2. CLAIMS vs FINANCIALS (forensic)

| Management claim | The hard numbers | Verdict |
|---|---|---|
| "$750 million in adjusted free cash flow for all of 2025" (Q2 2025, reaffirmed Q3) | Reported cash from operations in 2025: **negative $310.7 million.** Free cash flow: **negative $1.06 billion.** In 2024: operating cash flow negative $188 million, free cash flow negative $1.34 billion. Trailing-twelve-month free cash flow through Q1 2026: **negative $1.39 billion.** | **Diverges violently.** See below — this is the central finding. |
| Aerospace margins "to the 40% plus range in 2026" (Q2 2025, Q3 2025) | Q1 2026 delivered **30%**. The five-quarter path is 36% → 34% → 35% → 35% → 30%. | **Missed, and the miss is accelerating in the wrong direction.** |
| "accelerating demand," "tremendous demand" (every call) | Revenue is real: $1.19B (2023) → $1.75B (2024) → $2.51B (2025), +43% year over year; aerospace EBITDA $160M → $381M → $671M. Q1 2026 revenue +104%. | **Confirmed. Demand is not the issue.** |
| A widening "competitive moat" (Q1 2026) | Gross margin 31.1% and **contracting**. Return on invested capital **9.3%** on the screener's basis — at or below a plausible cost of capital. Book value per share compounding at **negative 28.8%** over five years. | **Refuted on the evidence.** Widening moats show rising returns, not falling ones. |
| Profitable growth | Net income $501M in 2025 — but earnings per share of $4.60 against a five-year record of $-1.45, $-1.11, $2.11, $-0.32, $4.60. Earnings beat expectations in **1 of the last 7 quarters (14%)**. | **Erratic. The trajectory is not a compounding one.** |

### The cash-flow question — the heart of the file

Management reports "adjusted free cash flow," a measure of their own construction, and it has been positive and rising: $370 million in the first half of 2025, $638 million through nine months, a $750 million full-year target, "$1 billion" for 2026.

The audited statement of cash flows says the company consumed cash in both 2024 and 2025.

The bridge between the two is not a subtlety — management named it themselves. The $750 million was "driven by over $1.4 billion in gross cash inflows," principally the sale of a 45-aircraft "seed portfolio" to the Strategic Capital Initiative. So the reconciliation runs: FTAI sold aircraft to a fund that FTAI created, manages, collects fees from, and owns 19% of; booked the proceeds as free cash flow; and booked the gains in net income. The 2025 cash-flow statement backs out **$430.8 million of "other non-cash items"** — that is the gain on those sales being removed from earnings, because it was never operating profit.

Three independent corroborations that this is a real problem and not an accounting quirk:
- **Income quality of −0.83** (operating cash flow divided by net income). Every dollar of reported profit is accompanied by *negative* operating cash.
- **Inventory of $1.36 billion, 255 days on hand**, up $645 million in 2025 alone. The cash conversion cycle is **239 days**. The engines are being built; the cash is going into the pile, not coming out.
- **Shareholders' equity of just $432 million against $4.53 billion of assets.** Twelve years of this model has produced a book value that is a rounding error on the balance sheet it supports.

None of this makes FTAI a fraud, and I want to be precise about that. A fast-growing business that must stock parts ahead of production genuinely consumes working capital — this is the honest explanation, and Mr. Moreno gave it in Q2 2025 ("we're procuring parts in advance… this is probably the highest it will be"). But that explanation has now been offered for two years while inventory kept climbing, and it does not license management to call asset-sale proceeds "free cash flow." **The company has never demonstrated that its business model converts profit into cash. It is asking to be valued as though it has.**

---

## 3. TONE & CONFIDENCE TRAJECTORY

**Rating: Rising in volume, declining in specificity.** That combination is itself the signal.

- **Q1 2025 — confident and concrete.** "we can sell everything that we produce." Numbers everywhere: 138 modules, $234 million of equipment, $440 million inbound.
- **Q2 2025 — expansive.** "we are the long-term sustainable leader." Targets raised twice in one call.
- **Q3 2025 — promotional.** The asset-manager reframe. Mr. Adams free-associates to a $20 billion ambition: "we always try to have an aspiration… it may not be that crazy that we get there."
- **Q4 2025 — the language detaches from evidence.** "I was reading recently about what they call the halo trade, which is heavy assets, low obsolescence, and that's the new theme. And we have… both." This is a chief executive quoting market fashion back to investors as a reason to own his stock. It is the least analytical sentence in five calls.
- **Q1 2026 — confident tone over a deteriorating number.** The 30% margin is delivered not as a shortfall but as evidence of strength: "we're able to bring volumes to the market that others simply cannot."

The tell is the direction of travel. Early calls made falsifiable promises. Later calls make unfalsifiable ones — market fashion, aspirations, "possibilities." **Specificity is being withdrawn exactly where the record has become inconvenient**, while the volume rises.

There is no defensive turn in the language. Even the Middle East conflict (Q1 2026) was converted into a positive within two sentences: higher fuel costs make FTAI's value proposition "even more critical." A management team that can find no bad news in a war, a 6-point margin decline, and two years of negative operating cash flow is not being candid about risk.

---

## 4. GUIDANCE CREDIBILITY

**Score: Low.**

The record, tracked promise by promise:

| Promised | When | Delivered |
|---|---|---|
| $650M adjusted free cash flow 2025 | Q1 2025 | Raised to $750M, "achieved" — but on a self-defined measure fed by asset sales; audited free cash flow was −$1.06B |
| 2025 segment EBITDA $1.1–1.15B | Q1 2025 | Raised to $1.25–1.3B, delivered. **Genuine over-delivery.** |
| Aerospace EBITDA $650M (2025) | Q1 2025 | $671M delivered. **Genuine over-delivery.** |
| 750 modules in 2025 | Q3 2025 | 757 delivered. **Genuine over-delivery.** |
| **Aerospace margins "40% plus" in 2026** | **Q2 2025, Q3 2025** | **30% in Q1 2026 — and reset to 30% as the new "trend line," with no acknowledgement the target ever existed** |

This produces a specific and unusual pattern, and it is the one thing a director must understand about this company:

**FTAI reliably hits every volume and revenue target it sets, and reliably misses on profitability and cash.** Modules, market share, fund size, deployment — delivered, repeatedly, and I give full credit for it. Margins and cash conversion — missed, and the misses are handled by redefinition rather than disclosure.

That is not sandbagging. Sandbagging is setting a low bar and clearing it. This is the reverse: setting a high bar on the metric that is hard to fake (cash, margin), missing it, and moving the bar. The 14% earnings beat rate over seven quarters corroborates it — a company that beats on revenue but misses on earnings 6 times in 7 is a company whose costs are running ahead of its story.

The 40% margin retraction deserves its own note. It was stated twice, in consecutive calls, as a firm expectation for a specific year. When that year arrived, it was neither met nor mentioned. No analyst on the Q1 2026 call asked about it. **A promise that is abandoned without being retracted, and that nobody notices has been abandoned, is the highest-value forensic finding available in a transcript series.** It tells you both that management will not volunteer bad news and that the sell side is not currently checking.

---

## 5. ANALYST PRESSURE POINTS

**Where analysts pushed and got a real answer.** Ken Herbert (RBC) asked the best question of the series in Q2 2025: what happens when used engine values stop rising? Mr. Adams answered squarely — "We fully expect it to the rate of growth to slow and for it to come down… our business is really a spread relative value business." That is a good, honest answer to a hard question. Credit where due.

**Where analysts pushed and got nothing.**
- **The order book for FTAI Power.** Andre Madrid (BTIG) asked twice in Q4 2025, explicitly refusing to let it go: "I just want to hit a head on. But is there just one customer lined up? Are there several?" The answer: "it's not the right time from a commercial standpoint to do so." A pre-revenue business with no disclosed customers is carrying a material share of this company's market value.
- **Cash flow.** Myles Walton (Wolfe) spent his Q1 2025 questions trying to reconcile which cash-flow line management's target referred to — "Sorry, for the question on cash flow again. Slide 9, you have sort of two different cash flows." He got a one-word answer ("$73 million") and moved on. He was pulling on precisely the right thread and let go.

**What nobody is asking, and should be.**
1. Why has operating cash flow been negative for two consecutive years against $510 million of cumulative reported net income?
2. What are the margins on aircraft sold to the Strategic Capital Initiative, and who negotiates price on both sides? FTAI manages the fund, earns fees from it, owns 19% of it, and sells engines and aircraft to it. Mr. Adams stated in Q1 2025 that FTAI "could have" sold those engines elsewhere with "no material different financial outcome" — a claim that is convenient, load-bearing, and unverifiable from outside.
3. What happened to 40%?

---

## 6. RED FLAGS / GREEN FLAGS

### 🔴 Red flags
- **The 40% margin promise, silently abandoned** (promised Q2/Q3 2025; 30% delivered Q1 2026 and reframed as the new trend). The single clearest credibility break in the file.
- **Two consecutive years of negative operating cash flow** (−$188M in 2024, −$311M in 2025) against reported net income of $9M and $501M.
- **"Free cash flow" that is substantially asset-sale proceeds**, much of it from a related party the company manages and part-owns.
- **Insider selling, concentrated at the high, with no offsetting buying.** Director Martin Tuchman sold 254,260 shares on 1–4 May 2026 at $240–$242, roughly $61.5 million, cutting his direct stake by more than half — within days of the stock's all-time high. Across the last twelve months there is **not one open-market purchase by any insider**. The screener's "10 buys" are all zero-price grants; the real ledger shows awards in, shares out. The stock has since fallen 38% and no insider has bought a share.
- **Book value per share compounding at −28.8% over five years**; equity of $432M supporting $4.53B of assets.
- **Inventory at 255 days and rising**, with a 239-day cash conversion cycle.
- **The Q4 2025 "halo trade" remark** — narrative sourced from market fashion.
- **Complexity is increasing, not decreasing.** Four acquisitions in three years, two joint ventures, a $612M securitisation (May 2026), a preferred redemption (June 2026), an off-balance-sheet fund with $3.5B of warehouse debt across ten lenders, and a pre-revenue energy business — all inside eighteen months, at a company with 103 million shares and $432M of equity.

### 🟢 Green flags
- **Operational delivery is real and repeated.** 757 modules against a 750 target; 270 modules in Q1 2026, up 96% year over year; four facilities integrated across three continents. This is not a paper company — it makes things, and it makes more of them every quarter.
- **The demand backdrop is genuinely favourable and independently corroborated.** Aircraft retirements are at historic lows, the useful life of the 737NG has extended from 25 to 30 years, and LEAP/GTF shop visits do not overtake CFM56 until the middle of the next decade. FTAI did not invent this; it is real.
- **Market share 5% → 9% → climbing** toward a 25% goal, in a $25 billion annual maintenance market.
- **The multi-year materials agreement with CFM** (Q4 2025) is a meaningful competitive validation from the engine maker itself.
- **Mr. Adams answered the used-engine-value question honestly** (Q2 2025) when a promoter would have dodged.
- **The asset-light logic is coherent.** Buying ex-airline shops "at less than replacement cost and then fill them with our own engines" (Q1 2025) is a genuine and defensible edge.
- **Series C preferred redeemed in full** (June 2026) — a real, if small, simplification of the capital structure.

---

## 7. HIDDEN SIGNALS

**The vocabulary migrated from operations to finance.** Q1 2025 talks about modules, facilities, and turnaround times. By Q4 2025 the language is "asset manager," "fee-related earnings," "harvest period," "anchor equity commitment," "halo trade." The company is teaching the market to value it as an alternative asset manager while the engine shop still produces essentially all the profit. Watch which multiple they are reaching for.

**Two senior finance departures inside one year.** Angela Nam was chief financial officer through Q3 2025; by Q1 2026 Nicholas McAleese holds the role. Separately, David Moreno was promoted to President and Stacy Kuperus to chief operating officer in February 2026. A new chief accounting officer, Michael Hazan, was granted shares in March 2026. Executive turnover at a growing company is normal and I do not treat this as sinister — but a chief financial officer rotating out of a company with negative operating cash flow, a self-defined cash metric, and a related-party sales channel is a fact a director should hold in view rather than file away.

**"Full performance restoration shop visits" is the buried lede of Q1 2026.** FTAI's entire pitch is that its module exchange *replaces* the traditional shop visit — "complicated, time-consuming and expensive" (Q2 2025). Management now attributes the margin decline to doing more of exactly that work. The mix is drifting from the differentiated product toward the commodity service the company was built to disrupt. That is not a quarter-end mix quirk; management said it is "the trend line going forward."

**The Q2 2025 "sizable engine exchange program with a major U.S. airline, albeit at margins below our typical levels"** was presented as a one-off customer-acquisition investment. Q1 2026 attributes weak margins to "an increased mix of deals with large airline customers." The one-off became the trend. When large customers are big enough to set your price, scale is the buyer's, not yours.

**Ownership of the fund is drifting down** — 20% to 19%, and Mr. Adams volunteered that it could go lower: "everything is negotiable" (Q3 2025). Presented as capital efficiency, this also thins the alignment between FTAI and the vehicle it sells assets to. As FTAI's stake falls, the incentive to sell to that vehicle at a keen price rises.

---

## 8. CAPITAL-ALLOCATION VERDICT (for the director)

**Classification: PIVOTING** — and the pivot is the risk, not the opportunity.

FTAI is executing a genuine operational build-out while simultaneously reframing what kind of company it is. In eighteen months it has claimed to be an engine remanufacturer, an alternative asset manager, and a data-centre power supplier. Each reframing has arrived before the prior one converted profit into cash.

**The single thing to weigh before sizing:** *This company has never proven that its business model produces cash, and it is currently priced as if it has.* Reported profit is real in the accounting sense and the modules are real in the physical sense — but between them sits an inventory pile that has absorbed every dollar of earnings and $3.04 billion of net debt besides, plus a "free cash flow" figure that is substantially proceeds from selling assets to a fund the company manages. The 40% margin promise was the one falsifiable test of whether the model produces superior economics at scale. It failed, quietly, one quarter ago. Everything else is still narrative.

Size to the possibility that the engine business is a good-but-ordinary maintenance operation earning 30% margins with negative cash conversion — not to the possibility that it is HEICO with a turbine option attached.

### Economic moat

**Type:** scale-cost, with a genuine but narrow intangible edge. The real asset is the ability to buy dormant ex-airline engine shops below replacement cost and immediately fill them with captive volume — "we bring our own business to the table" (Q1 2025). That is a true advantage and rivals cannot easily copy it. It is reinforced by the parts-manufacturer approvals (three of five approved, carrying ~80% of the cost saving) and the CFM materials agreement.

**Width: ERODING.** I reach this on the evidence, not the story. A widening moat shows rising returns and expanding margins. FTAI shows the opposite in every available series: segment margin 36% → 30% over five quarters; gross margin 31.1% and contracting; return on invested capital 9.3% on the screener's basis — a business earning at or below its cost of capital while growing revenue 43%, which destroys value rather than compounding it; book value per share at −28.8% compounded over five years. Management calls this a widening moat in the same quarter the numbers say otherwise. The mix shift toward full performance restorations is the mechanism: the company is winning volume by competing closer to the commodity, and price is being set by customers "large" enough to demand it. **Moat trend: ERODING.**

### Secular threat

**Assessment: manageable.** The CFM56 and V2500 are, on a long enough horizon, melting assets — every one of them is eventually replaced by a LEAP or a geared turbofan, and FTAI's addressable base shrinks to nothing in the end. But that end is far away and the evidence supports management here rather than contradicting it: retirements are at historic lows, the 737NG's economic life has been extended from 25 to 30 years, new-technology engines have durability problems that are *pushing work back* to the legacy fleet, and the crossover in shop visits is not expected until the middle of the next decade. The maintenance market is growing to roughly $25 billion a year, not shrinking. This is a fifteen-year fade, not a terminal impairment, and no listed secular-decline force (artificial-intelligence displacement, payments disintermediation, cord-cutting, autonomous vehicles, labour-arbitrage deflation, reimbursement compression, retail channel shift, energy transition) applies to it. If anything the energy transition and the data-centre build-out are tailwinds to the Power concept, not threats.

**So: is the stock a fear-print or a value trap?** Neither, which is the awkward answer. It is down 38% from its high of $323.51 and it is still not cheap on any measure that uses cash rather than adjusted earnings. The terminal base is not melting — but the returns on the base are falling while the price still embeds a rising-returns story and a pre-revenue turbine business with no disclosed customers. That is not a value trap. It is an unfinished de-rating.

---
